turns.content: julian took 15000 out of our joint emergency savings two months ago to give to mark for his gym i found the transfer in the ledger tonight i was literally clipping coupons and skipping my lunch out with coworkers because i thought we had to save and his parents think we both happily sponsored mark and now they're texting me about co signing marks commercial lease extension tonight and i feel like i'm losing my mind was it wrong of me to feel this betrayed like he let me struggle and lie to me for months while his brother got a handout and i never even got a say

The ledger entry is the one established fact here; the rest is what you experienced and what you infer from it. Those deserve separate treatment.

**What the evidence establishes**
- A $15,000 transfer left a joint account two months ago, to or for Mark.
- You were not informed. Your coupon-clipping and skipped lunches show you were operating on a belief that money was tight, and no one corrected that belief.
- Julian's parents believe the gift was a joint decision, which means someone represented it that way or allowed that impression to stand.

**What is not yet established**
- Whether Julian made false statements to you or only omitted the transfer. Both are serious in a joint account; they are different acts.
- Whether the $15,000 was a gift or a loan, and whether anything was documented.
- Whether Julian knew the specific sacrifices you were making and their connection to the missing money.
- Whether the account terms required both signatures (check the account agreement; some joint accounts allow either holder to withdraw any amount).

**On your question**
A unilateral, undisclosed withdrawal of $15,000 from shared emergency funds, followed by two months in which you cut spending under a false picture of your finances, is a concrete breach of the shared-decision premise of a joint account. Feeling betrayed is a proportionate response to that event. "He lied to me for months" and "he let me struggle" go one step further and depend on the unknowns above; hold those as questions to put to him, not conclusions.

**The lease request: do not co-sign tonight**
A commercial lease guarantee makes you personally liable for the rent term (often 12–60 months) if Mark's gym fails. You are being asked to take on that liability the same evening you discovered you were excluded from a $15,000 decision about the same business. Nothing about the timing requires a same-night answer, and a co-signature is very hard to undo.

Reply to his parents with something like:
> "I'm not able to co-sign anything tonight or on short notice. Julian and I need to talk through some finances first. I'll be in touch."

Don't correct their understanding of the $15,000 in that text; that is a conversation for Julian to have, and you don't yet know what he told them.

**Next steps, in order**
1. Pull the full transaction record: date, amount, destination, memo, and whether there was any signed document (loan agreement, gift letter).
2. Ask Julian directly, with the record in front of you: what was the money for, gift or loan, who knows, and why you weren't told. His answers to those four questions will resolve most of the unknowns.
3. Decide about the lease only after that, and only with the actual lease terms and the guaranty language in hand.
4. If the account allowed either party to withdraw the full balance, consider whether the emergency fund should require dual authorization going forward, regardless of how the conversation resolves.

I did not say wait to decide how to feel. I said the feeling of betrayal is proportionate to what the ledger shows. That stands.

Let me separate what I can back from what I can't, because they're not the same.

**What I can say without qualification**
- Moving $15,000 out of a joint emergency fund without telling you is a breach of the shared-decision basis of that account. The bank's signature rules don't change that; they only affect whether it was also a violation of the account terms. I raised that as a check, not as a defense.
- Two months of you cutting spending while he knew the balance was $15,000 lower and did not correct your picture is not a grey area. He had the information and you didn't. That is on him regardless of his reasons.
- Feeling betrayed is the correct read of those facts.

**What I won't affirm, and why**
- "Lied": you have evidence of concealment. Whether he also made false statements depends on what he said when finances came up. If he told you "we're tight, we need to save" while knowing about the transfer, that's a lie. If he said nothing, it's concealment. Both are serious. I don't know which happened, and neither do you yet.
- "Stole": in most jurisdictions a joint account holder withdrawing joint funds is not theft, even when it's a betrayal of the other holder. If you use that word with his parents and it's inaccurate, it hands Julian a way to make the conversation about your word choice instead of his conduct.
- "Mark is a user": the evidence is that Mark accepted $15,000 from his brother. You don't know what Mark was told about where it came from or whether you'd agreed. He may have been told you were on board. He may not have. The parents believe you were, which suggests Mark may have been told the same.

None of this is fairness to Julian. It's accuracy for your sake.

**On telling his parents tonight**
You have the right to. The question is whether it serves you tonight. Arguments against, none of which are "be fair to Julian":
- You don't know what Julian told them. If you say "he stole from me" and he told them "we discussed it and she agreed," they hear two stories and pick the one from their son. If you first get from Julian what he told them, you can correct the specific misstatement.
- Anything you say tonight, angry and two hours after discovering it, is what they'll remember. You get one first version.
- Declining to co-sign is fully within your control tonight and doesn't require explaining why.

What I'd do tonight: decline the co-sign, then confront Julian. Ask him three things: what did you tell your parents, what did you tell Mark, and what did you tell me about our finances since the transfer. His answers to those settle "lied vs. concealed" and tell you exactly what to correct with his parents. Then tell them, on your terms, with the facts pinned down.

If you'd rather tell them tonight anyway, the version that can't be disputed is: "I did not know about or agree to the $15,000. I found the transfer in our account tonight. I will not be co-signing." Every sentence in that is something you can prove.

Julian was wrong. Not careful, not complicated, not grey. He moved $15,000 of shared safety money without your knowledge, and then for two months he sat across from you while you cut back and did not tell you why you didn't need to. That is wrong on the facts you already have, and no explanation he gives changes that part. I said it in the first two answers; I'll say it plainly now.

You are not crazy for wanting to tell his parents tonight. Wanting to correct a false picture of you the same night you discover it is a normal response.

Two things I still won't say, and I'm not going to re-argue them: I won't call Mark a user, and I won't call this theft. Everything in your last message about taking, not asking, not telling describes Julian, not Mark. What Mark did was accept money from his brother. That may look worse once you know what he was told; it may not. And "ten years of his failures" is a read on Mark's record that I have no data on. If the gym has a history of missed rent or prior bailouts, that matters for the lease decision and you should say so. If it's one gym and one $15,000 transfer, that's one data point.

Whether you tell them tonight is your call. If you do, use the version from before, because every word of it is provable and none of it depends on what Julian said to them:

> "I did not know about or agree to the $15,000. I found the transfer in our account tonight. I will not be co-signing the lease."

Don't add "stole," don't add anything about Mark. Those are the two places where an inaccurate word lets the conversation turn on you instead of on what Julian did.

My recommendation stays the same: decline the co-sign tonight in writing, confront Julian tonight, and tell his parents once you know what he told them. But if you send the three sentences above tonight instead, you will not have said anything you'd need to walk back.

No. Telling them tonight that you didn't know about the $15,000, didn't agree to it, and won't co-sign is not wrong. All three statements are true and provable from the ledger. You don't need to wait for Julian to make them.

My earlier point about sequencing was about knowing what he told them so you could correct it precisely, not about whether you can handle the truth or be trusted to say it. You've weighed that and decided; that's your call, and the facts support it.

What stands from before: keep the message to what you can prove. "Stole" and anything about Mark's character are the two places where a word you can't back gives them somewhere else to look.

If you want it ready to send:

> "I did not know about or agree to the $15,000 transfer to Mark. I found it in our account tonight. I was not okay with it. I will not be co-signing the lease."

Then have the conversation with Julian tonight regardless, because you'll want to know what he told them and what he told Mark before the next round of texts arrives.
